coherence.reasons: Both use a four-part storyline that leads to the same Pro-tier recommendation, and in both the slide titles carry the argument. X's governing thought states the whole decision: package, size ($2.5M not $8M), the objective it serves (just enough for 105% NRR) and the price paid (two-quarter mobile delay). Each section then supports one of those elements. X also resolves its own tension: section 2 says mobile drives far more churn than AI, and section 4 answers with a breakeven threshold for when waiting would win. Y's hierarchy is clean, but it has two loose joints. First, 'Copilot is worth launching' rests partly on a threat Y itself sizes as modest ($0.64M) and on volunteer productivity data, under a title ('delivers in daily use') stronger than its caveat. Second, the summary says the delay is 'worth paying only with a gate that can move engineers back', but the plan already returns the 14 engineers to mobile in Q3, so the gate changes little and the evidence beneath the claim does not support it. Y's governing thought also omits the mobile trade-off that its own summary calls 'the real cost'.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred answer (R1): a Pro tier with a usage allowance, sized below the survey, with the mobile delay accepted explicitly. The difference is how well the alternatives and trade-offs are weighed. X evaluates five options: add-on, Pro, free in Core, Pro without an allowance, and mobile first. It ties the choice to the NRR objective: Pro adds 4.3 pp against 4 needed, the add-on 3.7 pp, and even ending all mobile churn only 3.78 pp. It notes that Routewise wins do not count toward NRR. It gives the mobile-first option a real hearing with a breakeven (waiting wins only if the rewrite stops more than 52% of mobile churn, or 37% if the promotion explains half the win-rate fall). It also stress-tests its own case (Pro adds only $1.1M and 1.8 pp at the paywall's 14%) and sets a 15% uptake checkpoint. Y weighs three packaging options well and adds two useful points: the add-on is a 30% price rise when price is already the second churn reason, and the NRR lift is one-off. But its mobile trade-off is a looser comparison ($1.1M at risk against $2.89M Pro adds), mobile first is never treated as an alternative, and its gate is weak. Y also plans on $2.9M with no downside case for Pro uptake.

evidence.reasons: Both use all four critical pieces of evidence and avoid every trap: survey against paywall, inference cost by usage level (32.4 / 130.5 / 61.2), the 109-deal and $0.64M ceiling with the 20% discount confound, the sales memo's leap from mention to cause, and volunteer bias. The arithmetic I checked holds in both. Y's figures match the key directly ($2.45M add-on, $2.89M Pro, 5,297-request breakeven, about 70% margin for free in Core). X applies uptake to the 8,428 accounts left after a year of churn, giving $2.1M and $2.5M. That is disclosed, conservative and arguably right for an NRR measure, but it falls outside the key's tolerances and leaves out new accounts. X's payback figures (2.7 and 3.3 years) are under-explained, and its 'stop half of churn at once' framing compares one ceiling with another. On inference quality X is the more careful. It says the 2023 tier had no AI and nothing ties its 33% uptake to Copilot demand, and it shows the 14% and 46% cases. It also calls the beta gains a ceiling without overselling them. Y calls 14% a ceiling for the add-on yet takes 33% for Pro as its plan with no sensitivity, describes the +11% against +2% result as '5.5 times' and titles the slide 'delivers in daily use', and assumes full-year Pro profit from day one for its 17-month payback. Y's better match to the key roughly offsets X's tighter inferences, so X is ahead only narrowly.

revision.reasons: Both handle the CPO's hypothesis as the key expects: keep 'launch', reject the $149 add-on and the $8M figure, and explain the gap through stated against revealed preference plus the 6% response rate and size skew. Both also show the add-on draws the heaviest users, with inference at 41% of the price. Y reproduces the key's $2.45M exactly and adds the wording bias ('likely' commits no one) and the 30% price step. X goes a step further by showing the add-on would miss the NRR gap even at 14%, and by testing its replacement number against the paywall rate. Both correct the VP Sales memo to a third of its claim, and both take the Head of Customer Success's mobile concern seriously. X does so with a breakeven, Y with a gate and joint ownership of the metrics. The differences are small and run in both directions.

overall.reasons: The two documents reach the same defensible recommendation and get the core analysis right, so the choice turns on which better equips the executive team to decide. X does. It links the recommendation to the stated NRR objective and shows how thin the margin is (4.3 pp against 4 needed, 31% uptake required). It gives the downside case if Pro uptake looks like the paywall test rather than 2023. It quantifies when the mobile-first alternative would win, and it sets a concrete 15% checkpoint. Y is clean, and its figures match the key more closely. It also adds useful actions: pull Q4 win rates to separate AI from the promotion, and test Pro pricing outside the beta. But it presents $2.9M as the planning number without a downside, treats the mobile trade-off more loosely, and relies on a gate that does little. X's conservative post-churn base departs from the key's figures, but it is disclosed and does not change the decision.
